title: Solve word problems by choosing multiplication or division

lesson.title: Multiply or Divide? Read the Story!

steps.say: You already know how to multiply a two or three digit number by a one digit number, and how to divide one too. Today we learn just one small thing: how to look at a word problem and decide which one the story is asking for.

Here is the whole secret. Draw a bar for the story and ask yourself one question: is the big total the missing piece, or do I already know the total? If you know the equal parts and the total is missing, you multiply. If you know the total and you are cutting it into equal parts, you divide.

visual.caption: Four equal parts, total is missing, so we multiply

steps.say: Let us try one. A hockey jersey costs twenty-three dollars, and the coach buys four of them. Draw four equal boxes, each one twenty-three dollars. The total is the missing piece, so we multiply. Twenty-three times four equals ninety-two. The coach pays ninety-two dollars.

Now watch out for a trap. Mia has eighty-four blueberries and puts them equally into six little containers. How many in each container? Lots of kids see the word each and jump straight to multiplying. But look at the story, not the word. Mia already has all eighty-four berries, and she is sharing them out. Sharing a known total means divide. Eighty-four divided by six equals fourteen berries in each container.

visual.caption: 84 berries shared into 6 equal parts, so divide

steps.say: And here is a lovely way to check yourself. Multiply your answer back: fourteen times six equals eighty-four. It matches the total in the story, so we chose the right operation.

visual.caption: 6 groups of 14 makes 84 — the check works

steps.say: So remember, do not let one little word decide for you. Ask the story: is the total missing, or am I sharing the total out?

lesson.answer: Total missing? Multiply. Total known and being shared into equal parts? Divide — the story decides, not the keyword.

practice.question: Emma picks one hundred and eight apples at a farm near Kelowna and packs them equally into nine baskets. How many apples go in each basket? First decide: multiply or divide? You can draw one long bar for all one hundred and eight apples and cut it into nine equal parts to help you.
practice.answer: Divide, because we know the total and we are sharing it into nine equal parts. One hundred and eight divided by nine equals twelve, so there are twelve apples in each basket. Check: twelve times nine equals one hundred and eight.
